questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state what a production function asserts
questions.stem: A plant's engineers tabulate weekly output against the labour hours, machine hours, and kilograms of material consumed in that week. Read as a production function, what does the table assert?

options.text: Each input combination can produce at most the output listed beside it
Every input the firm buys can always be increased to raise output
options.misconception: believes production functions require all inputs to stay variable

options.text: The output listed is the quantity the firm will choose to sell
options.misconception: confuses a technical maximum with a profit-maximising choice

options.text: The product's selling price is set by the same schedule
options.misconception: believes a production function determines the price of the product

questions.explanation: A production function states, for each bundle of inputs, the largest output that technology can deliver from it. It is a technical statement about what is attainable, and the word at most is what makes it a maximum rather than a typical result. It is silent on price: the same 500 kilograms of material could be sold at a high price or a low one without the table changing at all, which is why the selling price cannot be read off a production function. Nor does the table prescribe the firm's output choice, since that depends on what buyers pay and on what the inputs cost.
questions.hint: Ask whether the table describes what is attainable or what the firm will actually do.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the variable input in a stated short run
questions.stem: A bakery's weekly plan keeps its three deck ovens and the size of its shop floor constant, while the dough mixed each morning depends on the orders received. On this reading of the short run, which input is variable?

options.text: The number of deck ovens installed
options.misconception: confuses an input held constant with a fixed cost that never matters

options.text: Dough mixed each morning
The floor area of the shop
options.misconception: treats the building as a variable input inside the short run

options.text: The owner's own capital stake
options.misconception: believes owner capital must be reallocated every week

questions.explanation: The short run is defined as the stretch in which at least one input is fixed and at least one can be varied, so the test is which quantity the plan lets move. Dough mixed each morning is set by the order book, so it varies and it is the variable input. The oven count, the floor area, and the owner's capital are all held constant by assumption, which makes them fixed inputs for this period even though the owner could in principle alter any of them later. What matters is not how easily a change could be made but which changes the plan is treating as unavailable.
questions.hint: Look for the input the plan lets respond to demand rather than the one it holds constant.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute a marginal product from two output observations
questions.stem: A bakery's weekly log shows 140 loaves at 30 labour hours and 170 loaves at 40 labour hours, with ovens and material held fixed throughout. What is the marginal product of labour over that change, in loaves per additional hour? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Marginal product is the change in total output divided by the change in the input, so here it is 30 extra loaves over 10 extra hours, which is 3 loaves an hour. Working in units: total product rises from 140 to 170 loaves, a rise of 30 loaves, while labour rises from 30 to 40 hours, a rise of 10 hours, and loaves divided by hours is loaves an hour. Taking the 10-hour change as a single block is the assumption of a constant marginal product across the block, and the back-substitution checks it: 140 loaves plus 10 hours at 3 loaves an hour is exactly 170. Because a change over 10 hours alone would average away any variation within the block, the figure is a block average, not the marginal product at 40 hours.
questions.hint: Divide the change in loaves by the change in labour hours, keeping both units.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: read a returns to scale classification from a doubling trial
questions.stem: In an engineering trial a plant doubles every input it uses and weekly output rises from 400 to 1,000 crates, with the technology left unchanged. Taking the output factor as output after the change divided by output before it, what is that factor? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The output factor is 1,000 crates over 400 crates, which is 2.5, while the input factor is 2 because every input was doubled. Returns to scale is judged by comparing the two factors, and here 2.5 is larger than 2, so the plant exhibits increasing returns to scale: scaling up the whole plant buys proportionally more output than the extra inputs alone would suggest. The same conclusion can be reached by the ratio route: output per unit of input rises from 400 over 2 to 1,000 over 2 in scaled form, confirming the factor exceeds the input factor. This is a statement about all inputs moving together, so it says nothing on its own about what happens when only one input is added to a fixed plant.
questions.hint: Divide final output by initial output and compare the result with the input factor of 2.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Returns to scale versus diminishing marginal returns
questions.learningObjective: distinguish returns to scale from diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: One plant doubles every input and gets 150 percent more output back, yet a single extra worker added to a fixed crew of ten adds less than the previous hire did. How can both reports be true of the same technology?

options.text: A plant cannot do both, so one engineer has misread the trial
options.misconception: believes a technology must show one kind of return and not the other

options.text: Rising returns to scale force the last hire to add more than the first
options.misconception: believes scaling all inputs lifts the marginal product of every single input

options.text: One report varies all inputs at once and the other varies only one
The two reports are two wordings of one single variable law
options.misconception: believes returns to scale and diminishing returns are the same statement

questions.explanation: The two claims are about different experiments. Returns to scale asks what happens when every input rises together, which is the direction in which spreading setup, specialisation, and indivisibilities across a bigger plant can make output more than proportional. Diminishing marginal returns asks what happens when one input is added while the others are held at their fixed level, and with a fixed plant some inputs are crowded, so congestion eventually sets in. Because the two experiments move different variables, they can point in opposite directions on the same shop floor without either being wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what each report holds constant while the other thing moves.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: connect a negative marginal product to total product
questions.stem: A depot's shift log shows the marginal product of its sorters turning negative once the shift passes eighteen hours. What must the same log be showing about total packages handled?

options.text: Handling is still climbing at eighteen hours and will keep climbing
options.misconception: believes a falling marginal product still adds to total output

options.text: Handling is flat whenever the marginal product is negative
options.misconception: believes a negative marginal product leaves total output untouched

options.text: Handling has stopped rising but has not yet started falling
options.misconception: believes total output turns before the marginal product does

options.text: Handling peaked below eighteen hours and now shrinks

questions.explanation: Total product is the running sum of marginal products, so the sign of the marginal product says which way the total moves: a positive marginal product adds to it, a negative one subtracts from it, and a zero one leaves it flat. Once the marginal product is negative, each extra hour of sorting is taking away more than it adds, and the running total must already have passed its peak before the marginal product crossed zero. A marginal product that is merely falling but still positive raises total output by less each hour; it is the sign, not the slope, that tells you which way the total is heading.
questions.hint: Total output is the accumulated sum of marginal products, so read the sign.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Marginal product from a production table
questions.learningObjective: read a marginal product off a discrete production schedule
questions.stem: A plant's daily log records 40, 75, 100, 115, and 120 units of output at 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40 machine hours, with labour and material fixed. What is the marginal product of the thirtieth machine hour, in units an hour, and how does it compare with the first?
questions.explanation: The thirtieth hour is bracketed by the 20-hour row at 100 units and the 30-hour row at 115 units, so its marginal product is 15 units over 10 hours, which is 1.5 units an hour. The first hour is bracketed by 0 hours at 40 units and 10 hours at 75 units, so its marginal product is 35 units over 10 hours, or 3.5 units an hour. The sequence of block marginal products is therefore 3.5, 2.5, 1.5, and 0.5 units an hour, a strictly falling series while labour and material are held fixed, which is the law of diminishing marginal returns. Reading the rise in total output between 0 and 40 hours as a single block would instead report 2 units an hour and hide the fall.
questions.hint: Bracket the thirtieth hour with the 20-hour and 30-hour rows, then compare with the first hour's bracket.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute an average product at a stated output
questions.stem: A bakery bakes 180 loaves a day with 20 labour hours and 300 loaves a day with 40 labour hours, with the oven bank fixed in both cases. What is the average product of labour at 40 hours, in loaves an hour? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The average product is total product divided by the input, so 300 loaves over 40 hours is 7.5 loaves an hour. At 20 hours the same measure gives 180 loaves over 20 hours, which is 9 loaves an hour, so the average product fell from 9 to 7.5 as labour hours rose, the signature of diminishing marginal returns showing up in the average. Units carry through: loaves per hour for labour hours. Because the average product is a ratio it is silent about the level of output, which is why a bakery can double its loaves while its loaves per hour fall.
questions.hint: Divide total loaves by total labour hours at the 40-hour observation only.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the slope of an isocost line
questions.stem: A plant spends 3,600 dollars a week, buying machine hours at 24 dollars an hour and labour hours at 8 dollars an hour. Writing labour hours against machine hours, what is the slope of the resulting isocost, in labour hours per machine hour, ignoring the sign?
questions.explanation: The isocost is 24 times machine hours plus 8 times labour hours set equal to 3,600, so moving one dollar of spending from labour to machinery drops labour hours by 8 and raises machine hours by 24. The slope is therefore minus 24 over 8, which is minus 3 labour hours per machine hour, and the question asks for the magnitude. The intercept route confirms it: spending everything on labour buys 3,600 over 8, or 450 labour hours, while spending everything on machinery buys 3,600 over 24, or 150 machine hours, and the ratio 450 over 150 is 3. The sign is negative because both inputs cost money, so buying more machinery always means less labour.
questions.hint: Set total spending equal to the cost of each input times its hours, then read the slope off the ratio of the two prices.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a total cost low point is not an average cost minimum
questions.stem: A manager argues that the shop's average total cost must be at its minimum at 40 items a day, because total cost happens to reach its lowest figure at exactly that output. Explain why the reasoning fails, and state what the marginal cost comparison shows instead.

answer.exemplar: The reasoning fails because total cost and average total cost are different objects, and nothing forces them to bottom out together. Total cost is running totals that rise as soon as any further item is made, so its lowest recorded figure is just the smallest output the manager bothered to record, and it is a level rather than a rate. Average total cost divides that running total by the number of items, and a rate can fall while the level is still climbing. The relevant comparison is with marginal cost: the average total cost curve is falling wherever marginal cost sits below it and rising wherever marginal cost sits above it, and the curve is at its minimum exactly where marginal cost cuts through it from below. So a low total cost figure is no evidence at all about where the average turns, and the manager's claim is refuted by checking whether marginal cost is below or above average total cost at 40 items.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates the level of total cost from the rate of average total cost and then uses the marginal rule to locate the turning point, while a weak answer stops at asserting that the two differ. The tempting wrong version treats the lowest figure in a cost table as the cost-minimising output, which confuses a level with a rate. A second wrong version says the minimum occurs where the two cost curves intersect without explaining which two, or claims total cost stops rising at the minimum of average cost, when in fact total cost is still increasing there.
questions.hint: Separate a total from a per-unit rate, then ask whether marginal cost lies above or below the average.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Output choice and profit at a given price
questions.learningObjective: find the output choice and the profit it yields
questions.stem: A price-taking firm sells at 30 dollars an item and faces total cost of 100 plus 5Q plus one half of Q squared, where Q is items a day and cost is in dollars. First find the profit-maximising daily output, then report the daily profit that output earns.

options.text: Plus 212.5 dollars, having chosen 25 items a day
Plus 312.5 dollars, having chosen 25 items a day
options.misconception: omits the fixed cost from the profit calculation

options.text: Minus 100 dollars, having chosen 50 items a day
options.misconception: applies the shutdown condition in place of the profit-maximising rule

options.text: Zero dollars, having chosen 25 items a day
options.misconception: confuses earning a positive economic profit with breaking even

questions.explanation: For a price taker the profit-maximising rule sets price equal to marginal cost. Differentiating total cost gives marginal cost of 5 plus Q dollars an item, and 30 equals 5 plus Q gives Q of 25 items. At that output total cost is 100 plus 125 plus 312.5, or 537.5 dollars, total revenue is 30 times 25, or 750 dollars, and profit is 212.5 dollars. The second route agrees: average total cost at 25 items is 537.5 over 25, or 21.5 dollars, and the margin of 8.5 dollars times 25 items is again 212.5. The 312.5 figure is what you get by forgetting the 100 dollars of fixed cost, and the minus 100 figure comes from setting price against average variable cost, which is the shutdown test and not the output rule.
questions.hint: Set price equal to marginal cost first, then compute revenue minus total cost at that output.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the two horizons by which inputs are fixed
questions.stem: A bakery's owner complains that because she can add a fifth oven on Friday, the oven was never really a fixed input. Which correction identifies what she has mixed up?

options.text: An oven becomes variable the moment the owner contemplates another one
options.misconception: believes contemplating a change makes an input variable

options.text: A horizon is set by which inputs are fixed, not by how fast a firm acts
If ovens can be added, no short run can exist for a bakery
options.misconception: believes a short run requires every input to stay fixed for ever

options.text: The long run is simply the short run with a larger installed base
options.misconception: identifies a longer horizon with a bigger stock of machinery

questions.explanation: The two horizons are not distinguished by how quickly a firm can act or by how much notice it must give, but by which inputs are held fixed. In the short run some input is fixed by assumption, so the oven count is fixed inside the period no matter how readily another could be ordered. The long run is the horizon at which every input becomes adjustable, which is the only setting in which the oven count itself can be varied. Calling the oven variable the instant the owner thinks about a change confuses a possibility with an assumption, and a horizon is an assumption about what the model is holding still.
questions.hint: Ask whether the classification depends on what is adjustable or on how quickly the firm can act.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Fixed cost and the output choice
questions.learningObjective: state what a fixed cost does and does not respond to
questions.stem: A plant's controller argues that because the monthly factory rent is a fixed cost, the rent should be ignored when the plant picks how much to produce this month. Which statement about fixed costs refutes that argument?

options.text: A fixed cost per item rises with output, thinning as more are made
options.misconception: believes average fixed cost increases as production expands

options.text: A fixed cost is avoidable this month, so shutting down releases it
options.misconception: believes shutdown escapes a cost that the lease does not avoid

options.text: A fixed cost does not vary with output, so no output choice removes it
A fixed cost is a sunk cost, irrelevant to every decision for ever
options.misconception: treats a fixed cost as irrelevant beyond the period it is paid in

questions.explanation: A fixed cost is a cost that does not vary with the output choice, which is exactly why ignoring it when picking an output is wrong. The rent is due in full this month whether the plant makes ten thousand crates or ten, so no output decision changes it and no output decision can be justified by it. The cost that does respond is the variable cost, and the decision rule therefore looks at marginal cost, not at total cost. What the fixed cost does change is average total cost, because spreading it over more crates lowers the average; but lowering the average is not a reason to raise output.
questions.hint: Ask whether any output the plant could choose would make the rent smaller.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute average fixed cost at a given output
questions.stem: A workshop's daily overhead note lists 1,200 dollars of rent, insurance, and salaried supervision that are the same whatever it makes, and it made 50 items on Tuesday and 150 items on Friday. What is average fixed cost per item on Friday, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Average fixed cost is the fixed cost divided by output, so 1,200 dollars over 150 items is 8 dollars an item. On Tuesday the same 1,200 dollars spread over 50 items gives 24 dollars an item, so average fixed cost falls as output rises, which is the whole point of the measure: the same unchanged total is divided among more items. Units are dollars of fixed cost per item produced. The figure never falls to zero at any finite output, it only approaches zero, and it is unrelated to the marginal cost of one more item because adding an item changes variable cost only.
questions.hint: Divide the unchanged overhead total by the Friday item count.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute average total cost from fixed and variable cost
questions.stem: A workshop's daily report lists fixed cost of 900 dollars and variable cost of 40 dollars an item, and it makes 60 items that day. What is average total cost per item that day, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Average total cost is average fixed cost plus average variable cost, so the average fixed cost is 900 dollars over 60 items, which is 15 dollars an item, and adding the 40 dollars an item of variable cost gives 55 dollars an item. The second route agrees: total cost is 900 plus 40 times 60, or 3,300 dollars, and 3,300 dollars over 60 items is 55 dollars. The two components behave differently as output changes, since average fixed cost falls and average variable cost here is constant at 40 dollars, so the fall in average total cost comes entirely from spreading the 900 dollars thinner.
questions.hint: Add average fixed cost, which is fixed cost over output, to variable cost an item.

questions.topic: Marginal cost from a cost table
questions.learningObjective: compute marginal cost over an output interval
questions.stem: A bakery's accounts give total cost of 1,000 dollars at 40 loaves and 1,150 dollars at 50 loaves, with a new oven paid for inside that interval. What is the marginal cost of the loaves from 41 to 50, in dollars a loaf? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Marginal cost over an interval is the change in total cost divided by the change in output, so 1,150 dollars minus 1,000 dollars is 150 dollars over 10 extra loaves, which is 15 dollars a loaf. Units are dollars per loaf. The back-substitution confirms the block average: 1,000 dollars plus 10 loaves at 15 dollars is exactly 1,150. The oven payment matters for interpretation rather than for the division: an upfront payment is a lump sum inside the interval, so the 15 dollars understates the cost of the very last loaves and overstates the cost of the first ones, which is why true marginal cost rises across a step in fixed cost.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain the rising stretch of the average cost curve
questions.stem: A plant's average total cost curve falls, flattens, then climbs as output expands. What mechanism produces the climbing stretch at the right-hand end?

options.text: The fixed cost being spread thinner keeps pulling the average down
options.misconception: believes spreading fixed cost can push an average upward

options.text: Suppliers raise every input price as the plant's output grows
options.misconception: believes the rise in the average comes from general inflation

options.text: Averaging two curves always produces an upward bend on the right
options.misconception: believes the bend is an artefact of averaging two schedules

options.text: Rising marginal cost finally outweighs a fixed cost spread ever thinner

questions.explanation: Average total cost is the sum of two forces pulling in opposite directions. Average fixed cost falls without limit as output spreads the unchanged fixed cost over more units, and average variable cost typically falls at first and then rises once the plant is congested. Early on the thinning fixed cost dominates and the average falls; further out the rising average variable cost dominates and the average climbs. That is why the average total cost curve is U shaped and why the minimum sits where the two effects balance, which is also where the marginal cost curve crosses it from below.
questions.hint: Break average total cost into its fixed and variable halves and see which one wins at each end.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute marginal cost from average cost observations
questions.stem: A firm's quarterly table gives total revenue of 40,000 and 41,500 dollars and average total cost of 3.60 and 3.40 dollars an item at 10,000 and 11,000 items. What is marginal cost per item over that step, in dollars, and is the average total cost moving in the right direction there?
questions.explanation: Average total cost times output gives total cost, so total cost is 3.60 times 10,000, which is 36,000 dollars, and 3.40 times 11,000, which is 37,400 dollars. Marginal cost over the step is the 1,400 dollar rise over 1,000 extra items, which is 1.40 dollars an item. The average total cost figure of 3.40 is consistent exactly, since 37,400 over 11,000 is 3.40. Because marginal cost at 1.40 lies below average total cost at 3.40, the average is being pulled down, and indeed it falls from 3.60 to 3.40. Marginal revenue over the same step is 1.50 dollars, so the extra thousand items add ten cents a piece to profit, which is why the firm should expand.
questions.hint: Recover total cost from average cost times output, then take the change in total cost over the change in output.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why marginal cost crosses each average at its minimum
questions.stem: In a standard firm diagram the marginal cost curve crosses the average variable cost curve at that curve's lowest point, and does the same for average total cost. Why must the crossing sit at a minimum?

options.text: Marginal below the average drags the average down, and above lifts it
The two curves are drawn to cross at a minimum by drafting convention
options.misconception: believes the crossing is a rule of drawing rather than an implication

options.text: Marginal cost can only equal the average at one arbitrarily chosen output
options.misconception: believes equality of the two is a coincidence of calibration

options.text: An average can only begin to move after the marginal has already turned
options.misconception: believes an average always lags the marginal it is built from

questions.explanation: An average is a running total divided by a running count, so each new unit pulls the average toward its own value. When marginal cost is below the current average, adding that unit pulls the average down; when marginal cost is above it, the average is pulled up. The average is therefore falling before the crossing and rising after it, which means the crossing is exactly the minimum. This is why the minimum of average total cost sits where marginal cost meets it, and the same logic gives the minimum of average variable cost and the lowest point of the short-run supply curve.
questions.hint: Think of each new unit dragging the running average toward its own value.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: interpret the slope of an isoquant
questions.stem: A plant's engineers sketch the locus of every input combination that yields 1,000 units. Along that sketch, what does the slope of the curve measure?

options.text: The percentage fall in output when each input rises by one percent
options.misconception: believes the slope is an elasticity of output for both inputs

options.text: How much of one input can be traded for one more of the other

options.misconception: believes an isoquant carries price information directly

options.text: The rate at which the firm's fixed overhead is spread across output
options.misconception: believes an isoquant describes how fixed cost is allocated

questions.explanation: An isoquant holds output constant while one input is exchanged for another, so its slope is a physical trade-off: the extra units of capital that offset the loss of one unit of labour. That trade-off is the marginal rate of technical substitution, the ratio of the two inputs' marginal products. The slope is negative because, with technology unchanged and output pinned down, giving up labour can only be compensated by adding capital. Nothing about money enters, since prices belong on the isocost, which is what the diagram uses to find the cheapest point on the curve.
questions.hint: Ask what one input buys in terms of the other when output is held constant.

questions.learningObjective: name the law behind a shrinking isoquant trade-off
questions.stem: Moving along one firm's isoquant toward its capital-intensive end, each extra machine hour retires a smaller slice of labour hours than the hour before. Which principle explains that shrinking trade-off?

options.misconception: believes a price line can bend under a changing input mix

options.misconception: believes the trade-off reflects a managerial target, not technology

questions.explanation: The law of diminishing marginal rate of technical substitution says that as one input is substituted for the other, holding output constant, the units of the second input saved per unit of the first rise less and less. Convexity toward the origin is what makes isoquants bow inward, so a straight isoquant drawn everywhere would assert a technology with no diminishing trade-off at all, which is why an L-shaped isoquant is drawn for fixed-proportions technology. The isocost cannot cause it, since prices set the slope of a line and do not alter the curvature of a curve.
questions.hint: Ask whether the substitution rate is a technological fact or a price fact.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: separate the shutdown test from the exit test
questions.stem: A seasonal plant's owner asks whether the workshop should idle through a bad quarter or keep running at a loss. Which pairing states the two tests correctly?

options.text: Shutdown compares price to average total cost, exit to average variable cost
options.misconception: believes the shutdown and exit tests can simply be swapped

options.text: Both decisions use price against average fixed cost, which is one test
options.misconception: believes a single test against fixed cost settles both choices

options.text: Neither test matters, since the fixed cost is due in every scenario
options.misconception: believes a cost paid anyway can still decide whether to operate

options.text: Shutdown compares price to average variable cost, exit to average total cost

questions.explanation: Shutting down is a decision about the current period, where the question is whether operating covers the bills that stop when the plant stops, which is the variable cost, so the test is price against average variable cost. Exiting is a decision about the next period, where the whole cost including the fixed cost is avoidable, so the test is price against average total cost. Because a loss-making firm can be better off operating at a loss, the two tests can point in opposite directions at the same plant, and getting the pairing the wrong way round is the classic error in this area.
questions.hint: Ask which costs actually disappear under each choice before comparing price to anything.

questions.explanation: A natural monopoly is a market in which one firm can supply the entire output at lower total cost than two or more firms could, which economists call subadditivity of the cost function. questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why a single price cannot cover fixed cost
questions.learningObjective: explain the problem a two-part tariff solves
questions.stem: A water utility complains that no single price per cubic metre can pay for laying the pipes, because a price high enough to cover that outlay would keep every household from connecting. Explain what a two-part tariff changes and which of the utility's two problems it removes.

answer.exemplar: The utility is caught between two objectives a single price cannot serve at once: recovering a very large fixed cost, and not pricing the marginal cubic metre above what it costs to deliver it. A two-part tariff separates the money into two parts, a fixed connection charge and a per-unit price, so the per-unit price can be set near marginal cost and the fixed charge can be set to recover the pipes. The distortion is removed because households now face a price for extra water that reflects what extra water costs to supply, so they do not cut back on water they genuinely value, while the fixed charge does the cost recovery. The pair of problems is the same one that a natural monopoly faces, and the remaining objection is distributional rather than efficiency based: a large fixed charge falls hardest on small households, so it is often paired with a reduced rate for basic blocks. What the tariff cannot do is remove the fixed cost itself, and it cannot fix a monopoly that uses the fee to extract surplus from customers rather than to cover the pipes.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names both halves of the tariff and shows that the per-unit price can sit at marginal cost while the fee recovers the fixed outlay, then says what the fee's distributional cost is. The tempting wrong version asserts that a two-part tariff is simply a disguised price rise, which ignores that the per-unit price can be lower than the single price it replaces. A second wrong version says the tariff makes the fixed cost disappear, or that it is only fair for large users, when its real purpose is to stop the marginal price from being set above marginal cost.
questions.hint: Separate the charge for being connected from the charge for each extra unit, and ask which one was blocking the other.

questions.topic: Claim about the minimum of average cost

questions.stem: A manager states that the plant should halt production at the output where average total cost is smallest, since that is where the cost per item is lowest. Explain why a marginal cost comparison refutes the claim, and state the rule the firm should use.

answer.exemplar: The claim confuses the cheapest way of making a unit with the most profitable amount to make. Average total cost answers a narrow question, which is that at this particular rate of production each unit is cheap on average, and a firm can sit there and still be losing money if the price is below that average. The comparison that matters is between price and marginal cost, because the change in profit from one more unit is the price of that unit less what it costs to make, and the total of those changes is the whole difference between staying and expanding. If price stands above marginal cost at the low point of average total cost, then the average there is below price and marginal cost is below it too, so every further unit adds to profit and stopping at the average's minimum throws profit away. The rule the firm should use is to expand while price exceeds marginal cost, contract while price falls short, and shut down only if price falls below average variable cost, which is a separate question from where any cost curve bottoms out.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates the cost per unit from the profit per additional unit, and shows that the marginal comparison keeps moving output past the minimum of the average whenever price exceeds it. The tempting wrong version treats the bottom of the average cost curve as the goal because the average is at its smallest there, which mistakes an efficiency measure for a decision rule. A second wrong version says the firm should stop whenever price is below average total cost, which would have the firm idle while it could still cover its running costs and part of its fixed cost.
questions.hint: Ask whether the extra unit adds more revenue than it costs, rather than whether the average is falling.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: reconcile a falling marginal product with a falling long-run average cost
questions.stem: A workshop's short-run table shows each extra worker adding less than the last, while the owner's expansion plan promises a lower cost per unit once the floor space doubles. Explain why the two reports are consistent rather than contradictory.

answer.exemplar: The two reports hold different things fixed, which is the whole difference between them. The short-run table holds the plant constant and varies only labour, so congestion sets in: more people share the same machines, the same bench space, and the same supervision, and each one therefore adds less. The expansion plan lets every input grow together, so the firm is not asking the old plant to absorb a bigger crew but is building a bigger plant, and there the relevant law is returns to scale, which can favour enlargement while setup and fixed engineering costs are spread over more output. A falling marginal product within a fixed plant therefore says nothing about the average cost of a larger plant, and a planning note that read the short-run table as a verdict on the expansion would be reading a statement about one variable at a time as a statement about all of them at once.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the fixed input in the short-run table and points to returns to scale and spreading of setup costs in the long-run plan, showing the two hold different variables constant. The tempting wrong version treats diminishing marginal returns as a law that binds under every technology and horizon, and so declares the expansion impossible. A second wrong version assumes the expansion raises labour's marginal product simply by adding labour, ignoring that the added floor space is exactly what stops the crowding.
questions.hint: Ask what each statement holds constant, and whether the other quantities are moving at the same time.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Marginal cost from a rising cost table
questions.learningObjective: compute marginal cost from a discrete cost table
questions.stem: A plant's ledger gives total cost of 200, 300, 420, 570, and 760 dollars at outputs of 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40 units a day. What is the marginal cost of units 21 through 30, in dollars a unit, and is it rising?
questions.explanation: Units 21 to 30 are bracketed by the 20-unit row at 420 dollars and the 30-unit row at 570 dollars, so the marginal cost is the 150 dollar rise over 10 extra units, which is 15 dollars a unit. The back-substitution is exact: 420 dollars plus 10 units at 15 dollars is 570. The neighbouring block marginal costs are 10, 12, 15, and 19 dollars, a rising series, and the fixed cost of 200 dollars is included in every row, which is why it changes nothing in the differences.
questions.hint: Subtract the 20-unit total cost from the 30-unit total cost and divide by 10 units.

questions.topic: Fixed cost from two average cost readings
questions.learningObjective: recover fixed cost from average cost at two outputs
questions.stem: A line's cost record shows average total cost of 30 dollars an item at 10 items a day and 25 dollars an item at 20 items a day, and its variable cost is 20 dollars an item at both outputs. What is the line's fixed cost per day, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: At 10 items total cost is 30 times 10, which is 300 dollars, and the variable part is 20 times 10, which is 200 dollars, so the fixed part is 100 dollars. The 20-item row gives the same figure from the other direction: total cost is 25 times 20, which is 500 dollars, and the variable part is 20 times 20, which is 400 dollars, leaving 100 dollars again. That agreement across two different outputs is the check that the record is internally consistent, and it also shows why average total cost fell from 30 to 25 while variable cost per item did not move at all.
questions.hint: Multiply each average cost reading by its output, then subtract the variable cost implied by 20 dollars an item.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Long-run marginal cost by the rectangle rule
questions.learningObjective: estimate long-run marginal cost over an output interval
questions.stem: A firm's long-run cost record gives total cost of 25,600 dollars at 400 units a week and 34,800 dollars at 600 units. Using the rectangle rule, what is long-run marginal cost over that stretch, in dollars an additional unit?
questions.explanation: The rectangle rule treats long-run cost as linear between the two recorded points, so marginal cost is the 9,200 dollar rise over 200 extra units, which is 46 dollars an additional unit. The two averages bracket the answer as they should: long-run average cost is 25,600 over 400, which is 64 dollars, and 34,800 over 600, which is 58 dollars. Marginal cost of 46 dollars lies below both, and that is exactly the condition under which a falling marginal pulls a falling average down, which is what the two averages show. A rectangle-rule figure is an average over the interval and would be wrong at either endpoint if marginal cost is genuinely rising.
questions.hint: Divide the change in long-run total cost by the change in output, then check it against the two average costs.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Total cost at a given output
questions.learningObjective: rebuild total cost from average and average variable cost
questions.stem: A bakery making 30 trays a day reports an average total cost of 32 dollars a tray and an average variable cost of 27 dollars a tray. What is its total cost that day, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Total cost is average total cost times output, so 32 dollars a tray over 30 trays is 960 dollars. The other route splits the day first: average fixed cost is 32 minus 27, which is 5 dollars a tray, so the fixed part is 5 times 30, or 150 dollars, and the variable part is 27 times 30, or 810 dollars, and 150 plus 810 is 960. The two routes agreeing is the check, and it also shows the split a decision rule needs, since a price between 27 and 32 dollars a tray would leave the bakery better off running than idling while still losing money overall.
questions.hint: Multiply average total cost by output, then confirm with average variable cost times output plus the fixed part.

questions.topic: Long-run average cost at a stated output
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a long-run cost function at a given output
questions.stem: A plant's long-run total cost for the whole industry is 4,000 plus 30Q plus 0.06 times Q squared, with Q in units a week and cost in dollars. What is long-run average cost at 400 units a week, in dollars a unit? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Long-run average cost is long-run total cost over output. Total cost at 400 units is 4,000 plus 12,000 plus 9,600, which is 25,600 dollars, and 25,600 over 400 is 64 dollars a unit. Splitting the expression gives the same figure more usefully: the fixed-like part is 4,000 over 400, which is 10 dollars a unit, the linear part is 30, and the quadratic part is 0.06 times 400, which is 24, and 10 plus 30 plus 24 is 64. Long-run marginal cost there is 30 plus 0.12 times 400, which is 78 dollars, above the average, so the average is still rising at 400 units a week.
questions.hint: Divide the long-run total cost expression by output, then evaluate each term at the stated output.

questions.topic: Profit from price and average cost
questions.learningObjective: compute profit per unit and total profit at a price
questions.stem: A plant's long-run total cost is 4,000 plus 30Q plus 0.06 times Q squared, with Q in units a week and cost in dollars, and it sells 400 units a week at a price of 70 dollars a unit. What is its weekly profit, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Total cost at 400 units a week is 4,000 plus 12,000 plus 9,600, which is 25,600 dollars, and revenue is 70 times 400, which is 28,000 dollars, so profit is the 2,400 dollar difference. The per-unit route agrees: long-run average cost at 400 units is 64 dollars, so the margin is 70 minus 64, which is 6 dollars a unit, and 6 times 400 is 2,400. The margin route is the one that carries the decision with it, since a positive margin at 400 units is what tells the firm the output is worth running even though its long-run average cost is still below its average fixed cost share.
questions.hint: Subtract total cost from revenue, then confirm with the per-unit margin times output.

questions.topic: Recovering a cost function's fixed part
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a variable cost function and add fixed cost
questions.stem: A workshop's variable cost of making Q items a day is 30Q minus 0.2 times Q squared, in dollars, and its daily fixed cost is 800 dollars. What is its total cost at 50 items a day, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Variable cost at 50 items is 30 times 50 minus 0.2 times 2,500, which is 1,500 minus 500, or 1,000 dollars, and adding the 800 dollars of fixed cost gives 1,800. The average route agrees: average variable cost at 50 items is 1,000 over 50, which is 20 dollars an item, and 50 items at 20 dollars is 1,000 again. Marginal cost at 50 items is 30 minus 0.4 times 50, which is 10 dollars, below the average variable cost of 20, so the cost of the last items is low and the firm should cut output rather than extend it.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: find the output at which average total cost is lowest
questions.stem: A firm's total cost is 400 plus 20Q plus one quarter of Q squared, with Q in units and cost in dollars. At what output, in units, is its average total cost lowest? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Average total cost is 400 over Q plus 20 plus one quarter of Q, and differentiating that gives minus 400 over Q squared plus one quarter, which vanishes when Q squared is 1,600, so 40 units. The marginal check confirms it rather than merely repeating the first step: marginal cost is 20 plus half of Q, which at 40 units is 40 dollars, and that is exactly the average total cost of 40 dollars at the same output, and marginal cost always crosses an average at that average's minimum. The average falls before 40 units and rises after it.
questions.hint: Divide total cost by output, then set the derivative of that expression to zero.

questions.learningObjective: compute and interpret a marginal cost from a ledger
questions.stem: A plant's ledger lists total cost of 200, 300, 420, 570, and 760 dollars at 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40 units a day. What is the marginal cost of the first ten units of the day, in dollars a unit? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The first ten units are bracketed by the zero row at 200 dollars and the ten-unit row at 300 dollars, so the marginal cost over that block is the 100 dollar rise over 10 units, which is 10 dollars a unit. The 200 dollars at zero output is fixed cost and appears in every row, so it cancels in the difference and the whole 100 dollar rise is variable cost. questions.learningObjective: find the profit-maximising output and its profit
questions.stem: A price-taking firm sells 45 dollars an item against total cost of 400 plus 20Q plus one quarter of Q squared. First find the output that maximises profit, then report the profit at that output in dollars.

options.text: Plus 2,025 dollars, at an output of 50 units
options.misconception: adds total cost to revenue instead of subtracting it

options.text: Plus 225 dollars, at an output of 50 units
Minus 400 dollars, at an output of 100 units
options.misconception: uses the shutdown condition in place of the profit-maximising rule

options.text: Zero dollars, at an output of 80 units
options.misconception: stops at the break-even output instead of the profit-maximising one

questions.explanation: For a price taker the rule is price equal to marginal cost, and marginal cost is 20 plus half of Q, so 45 dollars gives 50 units. Total cost there is 400 plus 1,000 plus 625, which is 2,025 dollars, and revenue is 45 times 50, which is 2,250, so profit is 225 dollars. The 2,025 figure is the cost itself, which is the trap of adding the two columns instead of subtracting. The zero at 80 units is the break-even output, and the loss at 100 units comes from applying the shutdown test, under which price equals average variable cost, a rule that says whether to run rather than how much to make.
questions.hint: Set price equal to marginal cost, then compute revenue less total cost at that output.

questions.topic: Cheapest mix and what it costs
questions.learningObjective: solve for a cost-minimising mix and price it
questions.stem: A plant needs 100 units from an output function equal to the square root of machine hours times labour hours, with machinery rented at 40 dollars an hour and labour at 10 dollars. First find the cheapest machine-hour count, then report the total cost of that mix in dollars.

questions.topic: Minimum of average cost and its value
questions.learningObjective: report the output and cost at the minimum of the average curve
questions.stem: A manufacturer's total cost runs 400 plus 20Q plus one quarter of Q squared, where Q counts items a day and cost is in dollars. First find the output at which its average total cost is lowest, then report that lowest average cost in dollars a tray.

options.misconception: assumes average fixed cost is independent of the level of output

questions.explanation: Average total cost is 400 over Q plus 20 plus one quarter of Q, and it is smallest where minus 400 over Q squared plus one quarter is zero, which is 40 units, giving 10 plus 20 plus 10, or 40 dollars a unit.
